newsitem.title: UK: Dollar forges ahead unabated vs mark, yen in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar forges ahead unabated vs mark, yen in Europe.

text.p: The dollar forged ahead in European trade on Monday, rising to a 50-month high on the yen and its highest in three weeks against the mark.

Temptingly high yields in U.S. financial markets compared to those of Germany and Japan, European ministers' increasing determination to launch Europe's single currency on schedule, a flow of funds out of Japan at the start of Tokyo's new fiscal year -- all added to the dollar's charm.
"The interest rate differential factor and the EMU issue are firmly back in the dollar's favour, at least for the short term," said Chris Turner, currency strategist at BZW here.
"U.S. stocks stabilised on Friday and are up again today, and this is certainly helping as there has been a very strong correlation between the Dow and the currency," Turner said.

The dollar was at 125.75 in late European trade, just off a peak of 125.81 which was its highest level since January 1993. It was at 124.25 yen in late Europe on Friday. Against the mark it was at 1.7105, up from 1.6820 in late Europe on Friday.
Dollar bulls had been encouraged by the lack of discouraging comments by top-level U.S. and German officials in the face of the dollar's latest rally, traders and analysts said.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated on Monday that the dollar has been strong for "quite some time" and that this has helped the U.S. economy.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, speaking after a regular monthly meeting of G10 central bank governors in Basle, said there was no reason for concern about the currency market among the central bank governors.

"The fact that Tietmeyer didn't refer to dollar levels was definitely a dollar-buying factor. It made people think it was all right to keep on buying (dollars)," said Junpei Yamamoto, head of foreign exchange at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi in London.

Dollar/yen was also being helped by seasonal factors. With the start of Japan's fiscal year on April 1, investors there were keen to buy dollars to invest in foreign bonds for their higher yields, and the United States was an obvious magnet, traders said.

The U.S. Federal Reserve last month raised its key Federal funds rate to 5.50 percent and 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds now trade at a yield of 6.87 percent. Japan's key discount rate, by contrast, is a record-low 0.5 percent and among the lowest in the world. Yields on key 10-year Japanese government bonds are now 2.175 percent.
With dollar/yen having pierced an important level of 125 yen central bank intervention -- verbal or otherwise -- to stem the dollar was now the thought on most operators' minds.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see it (verbal intervention). Officials say it's in the U.S. interest to have a strong dollar but I don't think they want it to shoot up," BZW's Turner said.

"The 125 level was a key one both technically and psychologically, so the risk now is that it will spurt up quite sharply. We might see something quite soon in order to tone things down, even though they wouldn't want the dollar to collapse," he said.

Even so, economic fundamentals were so much in the dollar's favour that verbal intervention was unlikely to destroy sentiment, and the market would likely test 127 yen before backing off, BOT-Mitsubishi's Yamamoto said.

Dollar/mark was also boosted by growing perceptions that European monetary union was likely go ahead on time in 1999, which would mean replacing the mark with a currency which is seen as not as credible or stable.

Optimism over EMU weakened the mark across the board. Sterling rose above its old floor of 2.7780 marks in the European exchange rate mechanism for the first time since Britain dropped out of the ERM in September 1992. It was at 2.7817 marks in late trade against 2.7538 late on Friday.
